subsection: 1. The rock cycle and rock formation

notes.b: Rocks are continually formed, modified, destroyed and reconstituted. Endogenic (internal) forces form and modify rock; exogenic (external) forces destroy it; deposition of sediment reconstitutes it.
points: Endogenic forces, driven from within the earth, form and modify rock through magma, heat and pressure.
Exogenic forces, working at the surface, destroy rock through weathering and erosion.
Deposition of sediment reconstitutes rock as new sedimentary rock.

Cycle path: magma cools and crystallises to igneous rock; weathering and erosion produce sediment; deposition, compaction and cementation make sedimentary rock; heat and pressure make metamorphic rock; melting returns it to magma.
Short-cuts: any rock can be weathered, and any rock can be metamorphosed or melted.
Plate link: rock is created at plate boundaries and hotspots, metamorphosed at collision zones, and destroyed or recycled at subduction zones.
Diagram: a circular flow chart with magma and the three rock types as nodes, each arrow labelled with its process.

notes.b: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and crystallises. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface.
points: Crystal size depends on cooling rate: slow cooling gives large crystals, and fast cooling gives small ones.
Plutonic (intrusive) rock is igneous rock that cools slowly deep in the crust, so its crystals are large.
Granite is a plutonic rock built from quartz, feldspar and mica crystals.
Plutonic intrusions: batholiths are huge dome-shaped masses, dykes are vertical and cut across beds, and sills are horizontal and lie along bedding planes.
Plutonic rock reaches the surface only after the rock above it has been eroded away.
Volcanic (extrusive) rock is lava that cools quickly at the surface, so its crystals are small.
Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock and forms from runny lava.
Geotectonic settings: basalt forms at constructive (divergent) boundaries and hotspots; andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive boundaries.
Uses: granite is used as building stone, kerbs, worktops and headstones; basalt is crushed for road chippings and aggregate.

notes.b: Sedimentary rock is formed from sediment laid down in layers (strata), usually in seas, lakes, river basins and deserts.
points: Sediment comes from weathered and eroded fragments of older rock, from the remains of plants and animals, or from minerals precipitated from water.
Sediment builds up in subsiding basins, on continental shelves and along trailing (passive) margins.
Lithification is the conversion of loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
Compaction: the weight of overlying layers squeezes out water and air, packing the grains together.
Cementation: minerals such as silica, calcite and iron oxide, carried by groundwater, bind the grains together.
Many sedimentary rocks contain fossils, the remains or traces of past life.
Bedding planes are horizontal surfaces separating one layer from the next.
Joints are vertical cracks that cut through the layers.
Many sedimentary rocks are porous, holding water in the spaces between grains.
Clastic rocks are made of broken fragments: sandstone from sand, and shale from mud and clay.
Organic rocks are made of the remains of living things: limestone from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, and coal from plant remains that accumulated in swamps.
Chemical rocks form from minerals that come out of solution: rock salt and other evaporites form as seawater evaporates.

notes.h: Irish sedimentary rocks and the conditions of their formation
points: Carboniferous limestone (Carboniferous period, about 360 to 300 million years ago) formed when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea, where shells and skeletons built up the deposit.
Old Red Sandstone (Devonian period) formed in hot, semi-arid conditions from sand and pebbles laid down by rivers; its red colour comes from iron oxide.
Shale and sandstone of the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone.
Chalk lies beneath the basalt along the Antrim coast.
Coal at Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny, formed from plant remains in swamps; both are former coal-mining areas.
Rock salt is mined at the Kilroot salt mine, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim.

notes.b: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by great heat and/or pressure without melting.
points: The two factors that cause metamorphism are heat and pressure.
Minerals recrystallise while the rock stays solid, so the rock usually becomes harder and denser.
The rock may develop banding or cleavage.
Thermal (contact) metamorphism: rock beside an igneous intrusion is baked by its heat, forming a ring of altered rock called a metamorphic aureole; it is small in scale.
Regional metamorphism: heat and pressure act over huge areas during plate collision and mountain building; it is large in scale.

notes.h: Parent rocks and the metamorphic rocks they form
points: Limestone becomes marble.
Sandstone becomes quartzite.
Shale (mudstone) becomes slate, and with more heat and pressure becomes schist.
Granite becomes gneiss.
Quartzite forms Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow; and the Twelve Bens, Connemara.
Mica schist is found in Donegal and Connemara, and a metamorphic aureole of mica schist surrounds the Leinster granite.
Gneiss at Inishtrahull, off Co. Donegal, is about 1.7 billion years old and is the oldest rock in Ireland.

notes.h: Irish rock types and Ireland's geological past
notes.b: Ireland's rock types form a recognisable pattern across the island.
points: Limestone floors the central lowland, and Old Red Sandstone forms the ridges of Munster.
Granite outcrops in Wicklow, Donegal and the Mournes; basalt covers Co. Antrim; metamorphic rocks lie in Donegal, Connemara and Mayo.

Plutonic example: the Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, is about 400 million years old and is the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain. The Mourne granite is about 56 million years old.
Volcanic example: the Antrim plateau was built by lava flows about 60 million years ago, as the Atlantic began to open.
The closing of the Iapetus Ocean during Caledonian mountain building produced the Leinster and Donegal granites and regional metamorphism.

notes.h: North America: active and trailing margins
points: Active western margin: Pacific plates subduct beneath or slide past North America.
Volcanic rock: the Cascade Range volcanoes, including Mount St Helens in Washington state (erupted 1980), lie above a subducting oceanic plate.
Plutonic rock: the Sierra Nevada granite batholith, California.
Regional metamorphism affects the western mountain belts.
The San Andreas Fault, California, is a transform boundary where plates slide past each other.
Trailing eastern margin: there is no plate boundary at the coast, so there are no active volcanoes.
Thick sediments accumulate on the Atlantic coastal plain, on the continental shelf and in the Mississippi delta.
The Appalachians are old, worn-down fold mountains of sedimentary and metamorphic rock.
Granite: speckled, with large interlocking crystals.
Basalt: dark and fine-grained; it may form columns.
Sandstone: gritty grains, often reddish or buff, and layered.
Limestone: pale grey, and it may show fossils.
Marble: white or coloured, with sparkling crystals and no fossils.
Quartzite: pale, very hard and glassy.
Slate: dark grey, and it splits into thin sheets.

keyTerms.definition: Forces from within the earth that form and modify rock through magma, heat and pressure.
Forces acting at the earth's surface, such as weathering and erosion, that destroy rock.
Molten rock below the earth's surface.
Molten rock that has reached the earth's surface.
Igneous rock formed by slow cooling deep in the crust, with large crystals.
Igneous rock formed by the rapid cooling of lava at the surface, with small crystals.
A huge dome-shaped mass of plutonic rock.
A horizontal surface that separates one sedimentary layer from the next.
The conversion of loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock by compaction and cementation.
The squeezing out of water and air from sediment by the weight of overlying layers.
The binding of sediment grains by minerals carried in groundwater.
Metamorphism caused by the heat of an igneous intrusion, forming a small-scale metamorphic aureole.
Metamorphism caused by heat and pressure over large areas during plate collision and mountain building.
A ring of altered rock surrounding an igneous intrusion.

questions.prompt: Examine the formation of sedimentary rocks, with reference to Irish examples.
questions.model: Sedimentary rocks form from sediment, which comes from weathered and eroded fragments of older rock, from the remains of plants and animals, or from minerals precipitated from water. Weathering breaks the older rock down, erosion removes the fragments, and deposition lays them down in layers (strata) in seas, lakes, river basins and deserts, usually in subsiding basins. Sediment builds up in layers that are separated by bedding planes. Lithification turns the loose sediment into solid rock in two stages. Compaction: the weight of the overlying layers squeezes out water and air and packs the grains together. Cementation: minerals such as silica, calcite and iron oxide, carried by groundwater, bind the grains together. Organic rocks form from the remains of living things. Carboniferous limestone formed in the Carboniferous period, about 360 to 300 million years ago, when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea; shells and skeletons of sea creatures built up the deposit, and it covers most of the central lowland. Old Red Sandstone formed in the Devonian period in hot, semi-arid conditions, when rivers laid down sand and pebbles; iron oxide gives it its red colour, and it forms the ridges of Munster. Shale and sandstone at the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone. Coal at Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny, formed from plant remains that accumulated in swamps. Clastic rocks form from broken fragments: sandstone from sand and shale from mud and clay. Chemical rocks form from minerals that come out of solution: rock salt at Kilroot, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim, was deposited as seawater evaporated.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how igneous rocks are formed. Name one igneous rock and a location where it is found.
questions.model: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and crystallises. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface. The rate of cooling controls crystal size: slow cooling gives large crystals and fast cooling gives small crystals. Plutonic rocks form when magma cools slowly deep in the crust, so the crystals grow large. Magma can form batholiths, dykes and sills before it reaches the surface, and plutonic rock is exposed only after the rock above it has been eroded away. Granite is a plutonic rock; the Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, is about 400 million years old. Volcanic rocks form when lava cools quickly at the surface, so the crystals are small. Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock and forms from runny lava, at constructive boundaries and hotspots; the basalt of the Antrim plateau was formed by lava flows about 60 million years ago. Andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive plate boundaries.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly how rocks are changed by thermal metamorphism and by regional metamorphism.
questions.model: Thermal (contact) metamorphism happens when rock beside an igneous intrusion is baked by its heat. The altered rock forms a small-scale ring called a metamorphic aureole; for example, limestone changes to marble. Regional metamorphism happens when heat and pressure act over huge areas during plate collision and mountain building. The rock recrystallises while still solid, becoming harder and denser; for example, sandstone changes to quartzite.
